core_themes.name: Overfishing of lobster and crawfish stocks
core_themes.claim: Current stock assessments and landing trends show that lobster and crawfish stocks in English waters are being overfished and are not being exploited at Maximum Sustainable Yield levels.

core_themes.name: EU and biodiversity obligations at risk
core_themes.claim: Continued overfishing jeopardises the UK's ability to meet its EU obligations (CFP/MSFD) to achieve MSY by 2020 and its Biodiversity 2020 commitments for crawfish.

core_themes.name: Common-good market failure
core_themes.claim: Fishing is a common-good problem where private incentives to exploit stocks diverge from the social cost, leading to over-exploitation and ecosystem harm.

core_themes.name: Particular harm from landing berried (egg-bearing) individuals
core_themes.claim: Landing berried lobsters and crawfish imposes a disproportionately large external cost because it removes future reproductive capacity essential to stock recovery.

core_themes.name: Inadequacy of existing local measures
core_themes.claim: Current patchwork of regional IFCA bans and conservation reference sizes is insufficient and inconsistently enforced, leaving stocks exposed to overfishing beyond inshore limits.

core_themes.name: National ban as the preferred intervention
core_themes.claim: A national ban on landing berried lobsters and crawfish is the preferred option because it provides sufficient spatial coverage and resolves enforcement problems associated with local bans.

core_themes.name: Rejection of voluntary action
core_themes.claim: Existing voluntary v-notching legislation has not achieved sufficient uptake, so a further voluntary scheme is unlikely to succeed and cannot be relied upon.

core_themes.name: Rejection of IFCA byelaw approach
core_themes.claim: A full inshore ban through IFCA byelaws was rejected because IFCA powers only extend to 6nm, leaving stocks beyond that limit unprotected and enforcement problems unresolved.

core_themes.name: Rejection of a seasonal ban
core_themes.claim: A seasonal ban was considered but rejected because the variable and lengthy egg-carrying period of lobsters and crawfish makes it impractical to define an effective national season and would not deliver the expected conservation benefits.

core_themes.name: Costs versus long-term benefits
core_themes.claim: Although the ban imposes quantified short-term costs on business (lost revenue from berried landings) and government, these are justified by expected but unquantified long-term benefits from stock recovery and higher future landings, based on modelled assumptions.

core_themes.name: Legal mechanism for the ban
core_themes.claim: The ban will be implemented by amending the existing Statutory Instrument on v-notched lobsters under the Sea Fish (Conservation) Act 1967, applying to UK and Scottish vessels fishing in or landing into English waters, which supports simplification of the legislative landscape.

core_themes.name: Enforcement costs and responsibilities
core_themes.claim: The MMO and IFCAs will enforce the ban using testing kits and training, incurring estimated annual costs, with enforcement folded into routine inspection activity.

core_themes.name: Consultation to test assumptions and gather evidence
core_themes.claim: Key implementation assumptions, including on fisher behaviour and the effectiveness of existing bans, will be tested through a formal consultation and stakeholder workshops before the policy is finalised.
